title: Signal Reaches Every Server
statement:
A cluster has n servers labelled 1 to n. Each entry links[i] = [u, v, w] is a one-way link: a message sent by server u arrives at server v after w milliseconds.

At time 0, server start sends out an alert. Every server that receives the alert forwards it immediately on all of its outgoing links. Return the time at which the last server receives the alert. If some server never receives it, return -1.

There may be several links between the same pair of servers, and a link may take 0 ms.

examples.why: Server 1 hears the alert at 5 through 2 → 3 → 1, not at 9 over the direct link. Server 4 then hears it at 5 + 1 = 6, sooner than 2 + 8 = 10 through server 3. The last arrival is 6.
Links are one-way. Server 3 can send to 2, but nothing ever sends to 3.
The only server already has the alert at time 0.

hints: The answer is the largest of the n arrival times. So the real task is: what is the earliest arrival time at every server?
Breadth-first search finds the fewest hops, not the least time. Which server's arrival time can you be completely sure of at any moment?

Of all servers not yet settled, the one with the smallest tentative arrival time cannot be improved, because every other route to it would pass through something that arrives later. Keep tentative times in a min-heap, settle the smallest, relax its outgoing links, repeat (Dijkstra).

explain.intuition:
Each server hears the alert at the length of its shortest path from start, and the answer is the largest of those, or -1 if one is infinite. So this is single-source shortest paths with non-negative weights, which is exactly what Dijkstra's algorithm solves.

The key fact: among the servers whose time is still tentative, the one with the smallest tentative time is already final. Any other route to it would leave the settled area through some other tentative server, which already costs at least as much, and weights never go down. So settle that server, then relax its links: for each u → v of weight w, if time[u] + w beats time[v], lower it.

Why a heap? Finding the smallest tentative time by scanning all n servers costs O(n) per step, O(n²) overall. A min-heap hands it out in O(log n). Why skip stale entries? JavaScript and Python heaps cannot lower a key in place, so when a time improves we simply push a second entry. The older, larger entry is still in the heap. When it is popped, its time is bigger than the recorded best, and we ignore it. Why must weights be non-negative? The "smallest is final" argument assumes that extending a path never makes it cheaper. A negative link breaks that: a server settled at 5 could later be reached at 3 through a detour, and Dijkstra never revisits it. With negative weights you need Bellman-Ford.
steps: Build an adjacency list: adj[u] holds (v, w) pairs.
Set time[start] = 0 and every other time to infinity. Push (0, start) onto a min-heap.
Pop (t, u). If t > time[u], it is a stale entry: skip it. Otherwise u is settled at time t.
For each link u → v with weight w: if t + w < time[v], set time[v] = t + w and push (time[v], v).
When the heap is empty, if fewer than n servers were settled return -1, else return the time of the last one settled (they come out in increasing order).
pitfalls: Using plain BFS or keeping the first time a server is discovered. Example 1: server 1 is first discovered at 9 over the direct link, but its real time is 5.
Forgetting the stale-entry check. The answer usually stays right, but every outdated entry relaxes its links again, which can blow up the running time.
Returning the sum of the times, or the time of the last server pushed, instead of the maximum shortest time.

complexity.time: O((n + E) log E), where E is the number of links

solutions.title: Bellman-Ford
solutions.idea: Relax every link, n − 1 times over (stop early once a full pass changes nothing). A shortest path has at most n − 1 links, so that many passes are enough. Works even with negative weights, but is slow.

solutions.title: Dijkstra with a min-heap
solutions.idea: Always settle the server with the smallest tentative time, relax its links, and skip heap entries that have gone stale.

followups: One link is allowed to have a negative delay (but there is no negative cycle). Which algorithm do you switch to, and why does Dijkstra give a wrong answer?
The cluster is dense: about n² links. Is the heap still the best choice, or does an O(n²) array scan win?
Return the actual chain of servers that carries the alert to the last server. What extra array do you keep?
